kahneman2004.citation: Kahneman, D., Krueger, A. B., Schkade, D. A., Schwarz, N., & Stone, A. A. (2004). A survey method for characterizing daily life experience: The day reconstruction method. Science, 306(5702), 1776-1780.
kahneman2004.design: Day Reconstruction Method: respondents rebuilt the previous (working) day as episodes, ticked one or more of 16 activities per episode, and rated 12 affect descriptors from 0 to 6.
kahneman2004.population: 909 employed women who worked on the reference day (from a convenience sample of 1,018); mean age 38; mean household income $54,700.
kahneman2004.verification: Table 1 transcribed from the published article PDF (page 1777) into drm_table1.csv.

atus2014_2016.citation: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. American Time Use Survey microdata, 2014-2016 (activity summary, respondent and ATUS-CPS files).
atus2014_2016.mirror: https://github.com/cran/atus (CRAN package atus 0.2, redistributed with BLS permission; commit 1049d1d6f3857f221d3907f73df909cab20de5bb)
atus2014_2016.design: Nationally representative 24-hour time diary; one randomly selected person age 15+ per household, previous day, primary activity only, weighted with TUFNWGTP.
atus2014_2016.verification: Estimates recomputed from the microdata by derive_atus.py. The same code on 2015 alone reproduces the BLS 2015 release: TV 0.7985 x 208.8 min = 2.78 h/day (BLS: 2.8 h), socializing 0.3808 x 106.9 min = 40.7 min/day (BLS: 41 min).

liu2023.citation: Liu, P. J., Rim, S., Min, L., & Min, K. E. (2023). The surprise of reaching out: Appreciated more than we think. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 124(4), 754-771.
liu2023.finding: Across preregistered experiments, people who reached out to someone in their social circle underestimated how much the recipient appreciated it.
liu2023.verification: Abstract-level finding only; no effect sizes are shown.

kumar2018.citation: Kumar, A., & Epley, N. (2018). Undervaluing gratitude: Expressers misunderstand the consequences of showing appreciation. Psychological Science, 29(9).
kumar2018.finding: People who wrote gratitude letters underestimated how surprised and positive recipients would feel, and overestimated how awkward recipients would feel.

boothby2021.citation: Boothby, E. J., & Bohns, V. K. (2021). Why a simple act of kindness is not as simple as it seems: Underestimating the positive impact of our compliments on others. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 47(5), 826-840.
boothby2021.finding: Compliment givers underestimated how positively recipients would feel and overestimated how bothered and uncomfortable they would be.

epley2014.citation: Epley, N., & Schroeder, J. (2014). Mistakenly seeking solitude. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 143(5), 1980-1999.
epley2014.finding: Train and bus commuters told to talk with a stranger reported a more positive, and no less productive, commute than those told to sit in solitude; separate participants predicted the opposite.

kardas2022.citation: Kardas, M., Kumar, A., & Epley, N. (2022). Overly shallow?: Miscalibrated expectations create a barrier to deeper conversation. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 122(3), 367-398.
kardas2022.finding: Deep conversations between strangers felt less awkward and created more connection and happiness than participants expected.

levitt2021.citation: Levitt, S. D. (2021). Heads or tails: The impact of a coin toss on major life decisions and subsequent happiness. Review of Economic Studies, 88(1), 378-405.
levitt2021.finding: Undecided people told by a coin toss to make an important change (e.g. quit a job, end a relationship) were more likely to make it, and those who changed reported being happier two and six months later. Participants were self-selected.

gilbert2002.citation: Gilbert, D. T., & Ebert, J. E. J. (2002). Decisions and revisions: The affective forecasting of changeable outcomes. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 82(4), 503-514.
gilbert2002.finding: People preferred decisions they could change, but those who could change their minds liked their outcome less than those who could not. Reversibility is cheap to exercise, not free.

gilovich1995.citation: Gilovich, T., & Medvec, V. H. (1995). The experience of regret: What, when, and why. Psychological Review, 102(2), 379-395.
gilovich1995.finding: Regrets of action dominate in the short term; regrets of inaction dominate in the long term.

richardson2023.citation: Richardson, J., & Gilovich, T. (2023). A very public replication of the temporal pattern to people's regrets.
richardson2023.finding: Replicated the interaction between action/inaction and time perspective, though the exact pattern differed from the original.

masicampo2011.citation: Masicampo, E. J., & Baumeister, R. F. (2011). Consider it done! Plan making can eliminate the cognitive effects of unfulfilled goals. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 101(4), 667-683.
masicampo2011.finding: Unfulfilled goals produced intrusive thoughts and interference on unrelated tasks; writing a specific plan removed those effects without completing the goal.

killingsworth2010.citation: Killingsworth, M. A., & Gilbert, D. T. (2010). A wandering mind is an unhappy mind. Science, 330(6006), 932.
killingsworth2010.finding: Among 2,250 adults sampled by smartphone, minds wandered in 46.9% of samples, and people were less happy when their minds wandered.

mark2008.citation: Mark, G., Gudith, D., & Klocke, U. (2008). The cost of interrupted work: More speed and stress. Proceedings of CHI 2008, 107-110.
mark2008.finding: Interrupted people finished tasks faster with no loss of quality, but reported more stress, frustration, time pressure and effort.
